content: The elbow joint is classified as a hinge joint, also known as a ginglymus. It is formed by three bones: the humerus of the upper arm, and the paired radius and ulna of the forearm. The bony prominence at the tip of the elbow is the olecranon process of the ulna. Movements Two primary movements occur at the elbow joint: 1. Flexion and extension, which involve the bending and straightening of the elbow, occur at the articulation between the humerus and the ulna. 2. Pronation and supination, which involve the rotation of the forearm, occur at the articulation between the radius and the ulna. This movement also involves the wrist joint. In the anatomical position (forearm supine), the radius and ulna lie parallel to each other. During pronation, the ulna remains stationary while the radius rotates around it at both the wrist and elbow joints. In the prone position, the radius and ulna appear crossed. Most of the force transmitted through the elbow joint is between the humerus and the ulna, with minimal force transmitted between the humerus and the radius. In contrast, at the wrist joint, most of the force is transmitted between the radius and the carpus, with the ulna playing a minimal role. Muscles, Arteries, and Nerves The muscles associated with the elbow joint include: Anteriorly: The brachialis muscle. Posteriorly: The triceps brachii and anconeus muscles. Laterally: The supinator muscle and the common tendon of origin for the extensor muscles. Medially: The common tendon of origin for the flexor muscles and the flexor carpi ulnaris. The arterial supply to the elbow joint is derived from an anastomotic network formed by branches of the brachial artery (profunda brachii, superior and inferior ulnar collateral branches) and branches of the ulnar and radial arteries (anterior, posterior, and interosseous recurrent branches). This network ensures a robust blood supply to the joint. The nerve supply to the elbow joint includes: A branch from the ulnar nerve as it passes between the medial condyle and the olecranon. A filament from the musculocutaneous nerve. Two branches from the median nerve. Portions of the Joint The elbow joint consists of three distinct portions, all of which are enclosed within a common synovial membrane. The movements of the entire joint should be studied together, as the combination of forearm flexion and extension with hand pronation and supination is essential for the precision of fine hand movements. The hand articulates directly with the distal surface of the radius, while the ulnar notch of the radius moves around the lower end of the ulna. The ulna is excluded from the wrist joint by the presence of an articular disk. The rotation of the radial head around its axis imparts a circular motion to the hand through a significant arc. Ligaments The trochlea of the humerus fits into the semilunar notch of the ulna, while the capitulum of the humerus articulates with the fovea on the head of the radius. These articulating surfaces are connected by a capsule, which is thickened medially and laterally, and to a lesser extent, anteriorly and posteriorly. These thickened portions are described as distinct ligaments, including: The ulnar collateral ligament. The radial collateral ligament. The annular ligament. Synovial Membrane The synovial membrane of the elbow joint is extensive. It extends from the margins of the articular surfaces of the humerus and lines the coronoid, radial, and olecranon fossae. It reflects over the deep surface of the capsule and forms a pouch between the radial notch, the deep surface of the annular ligament, and the circumference of the radial head. A crescent-shaped fold of synovial membrane projects between the radius and ulna into the joint cavity, suggesting a division into two parts: the humeroradial and humeroulnar joints. Between the capsule and the synovial membrane are three fat pads: The largest fat pad lies over the olecranon fossa and is compressed into the fossa by the triceps brachii during flexion. The second fat pad lies over the coronoid fossa. The third fat pad lies over the radial fossa and is compressed into their respective fossae by the brachialis during extension. Terminology: Elbow and Ell The obsolete unit of length known as the ell is closely related to the elbow. This connection is evident in the Germanic origins of the words Elle (ell, defined as the length of an arm from shoulder to fingertips) and Ellenbogen (elbow). It is unclear when or why the second l was dropped from the English usage of the word. A more precise spelling would be ellbow for the joint and ellbone for the ulna, the etymological origin of both the unit and the joint. Carrying Angle When the arm is extended with the palm facing forward or upward, the bones of the humerus and forearm are not perfectly aligned. There is a deviation from a straight line, typically between 5-10°, in the direction of the thumb. This deviation is referred to as the carrying angle. In females, the carrying angle is generally greater than in males. The carrying angle can influence how objects are held, as individuals with a more pronounced carrying angle may supinate the forearm more when holding objects to keep the elbow closer to the body.
